Content:
Recall that the line integral with respect to arc length of a function [MATH: f(x,y)] along a curve [MATH: C] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t,]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] for [MATH: a \leq t \leq b] is a parametrization of the curve [MATH: C.]

Content:
In this lesson, we will consider the case when the curve [MATH: C] is an ellipse. To calculate a line integral along an ellipse, we need to parameterize the ellipse.

Content:
Remember that an ellipse with center [MATH: O,] horizontal semi-axis [MATH: a,] and vertical semi-axis [MATH: b] can be parameterized as
[MATH: \mathbf r(t) = \langle a\cos t,\: b\sin t\rangle, \qquad 0\leq t \lt 2\pi.]

Content:
Additionally, the direction in which we traverse our ellipse does not matter, because line integrals with respect to arc length are independent of the choice of orientation.

sections.normalized_html:
We will use the formula [MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.]

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form [MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{4^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{1^2} = 1.]

So, the curve [MATH: C] is an ellipse centered at [MATH: O] with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of [MATH: 4] and [MATH: 1,] respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle 4\cos{t}, \: \sin{t} \right\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \lt 2\pi.]

Computing [MATH: \mathbf{r}'(t)] and [MATH: \| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,] we get following: [MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(4\cos t)i + (d)/(dt)(\sin t)j; = − 4\sin ti + \cos tj; ‖r^{′}(t)‖|= sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2}); = sqrt((− 4\sin t)^{2} + (\cos t)^{2}); = sqrt(16\sin^{2} t + \cos^{2} t); = sqrt(15\sin^{2} t + (\sin^{2} t + \cos^{2} t)); = sqrt(15\sin^{2} t + 1)]

Now, since [MATH: f(x,y) = \dfrac{x}{y},] we obtain [MATH: f(r(t))|= (4\cos t)/(\sin t) = 4\cot t.]

Therefore, we can write the integral as [MATH: ∫_(C)(x)/(y)ds|= ∫_{0}^{2π}f(r(t))‖r^{′}(t)‖dt; = ∫_{0}^{2π}4\cot tsqrt(15\sin^{2} t + 1)dt; = 4∫_{0}^{2π}\cot tsqrt(15\sin^{2} t + 1)dt.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that the line integral with respect to arc length of a function [MATH: f(x,y)] along a curve [MATH: C] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t,]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] for [MATH: a \leq t \leq b] is a parametrization of the curve [MATH: C.]

Content:
In this lesson, we will consider the case when the curve [MATH: C] is an ellipse. To calculate a line integral along an ellipse, we need to parameterize the ellipse.

Content:
Remember that an ellipse with center [MATH: O,] horizontal semi-axis [MATH: a,] and vertical semi-axis [MATH: b] can be parameterized as
[MATH: \mathbf r(t) = \langle a\cos t,\: b\sin t\rangle, \qquad 0\leq t \lt 2\pi.]

Content:
Additionally, the direction in which we traverse our ellipse does not matter, because line integrals with respect to arc length are independent of the choice of orientation.

---

Item 2 — Example: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over an Ellipse

Example Prompt:
What expression is equivalent to [MATH: \displaystyle \int_\limits{C} \dfrac{x}{y} \: \textrm{d}s,] where [MATH: C] is the ellipse [MATH: x^2 + 16y^2 = 16,] traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We will use the formula
[MATH: \int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.]

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form
[MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{4^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{1^2} = 1.]

So, the curve [MATH: C] is an ellipse centered at [MATH: O] with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of [MATH: 4] and [MATH: 1,] respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as
[MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle 4\cos{t}, \: \sin{t} \right\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \lt 2\pi.]

Computing [MATH: \mathbf{r}'(t)] and [MATH: \| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,] we get following:
[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(4\cos t)i + (d)/(dt)(\sin t)j; = − 4\sin ti + \cos tj; ‖r^{′}(t)‖|= sqrt(((dx)/(dt))^{2} + ((dy)/(dt))^{2}); = sqrt((− 4\sin t)^{2} + (\cos t)^{2}); = sqrt(16\sin^{2} t + \cos^{2} t); = sqrt(15\sin^{2} t + (\sin^{2} t + \cos^{2} t)); = sqrt(15\sin^{2} t + 1)]

Now, since [MATH: f(x,y) = \dfrac{x}{y},] we obtain
[MATH: f(r(t))|= (4\cos t)/(\sin t) = 4\cot t.]

Therefore, we can write the integral as
[MATH: ∫_(C)(x)/(y)ds|= ∫_{0}^{2π}f(r(t))‖r^{′}(t)‖dt; = ∫_{0}^{2π}4\cot tsqrt(15\sin^{2} t + 1)dt; = 4∫_{0}^{2π}\cot tsqrt(15\sin^{2} t + 1)dt.]

Computing [MATH: \mathbf{r}'(t)] and [MATH: \| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,] we get following:
